title: Sorting algorithms
description: Seven ways to order a sequence: invariants, recurrences, and the cost of choosing a pivot.

topics.title: Bubblesort
topics.summary: Repeated adjacent comparisons move the next smallest element into the sorted prefix.
points: The lecture scans the inner loop from right to left. After outer iteration i, A[1:i] contains the i smallest elements in order.
With fixed loops, both sorted and reverse-sorted inputs take Θ(n²) time. Stable when equal elements are not swapped; in-place.
topics.example: [7,16,5,25] → [5,7,16,25] after the first full right-to-left pass.

excerpt.text: A[1 : i − 1] contains i − 1 smallest elements of original A, in sorted order

topics.pitfall: Do not claim the fixed-loop lecture version has a linear best case; that requires an early-exit modification.

topics.title: Insertion Sort
topics.summary: Insert each new element into an already sorted prefix. Study supplement: these slides refer to the textbook for insertion sort.
points: Before iteration j, A[1:j−1] is sorted; save A[j], shift larger values one position right, then insert the saved key.
Best case Θ(n), worst case Θ(n²). Stable with strict > in the shift test; in-place.
topics.example: [4,2,3] → [2,4,3] → [2,3,4]. In the second insertion, only 4 shifts.

excerpt.text: Detailed analysis of Bubble Sort [book does Insertion Sort]

topics.pitfall: Keep the key in a temporary variable before shifting, or its value is overwritten.

topics.title: Mergesort
topics.summary: Split in half, recursively sort each half, then merge two sorted lists.
points: Merge repeatedly takes the smaller front element from the two sorted halves in Θ(n) total time.
Θ(n log n) runtime. Standard array implementation uses Θ(n) auxiliary space; stable when ties come from the left half first.
topics.example: [8,3,5,1] splits into [8,3] and [5,1]; sort to [3,8] and [1,5]; merge to [1,3,5,8].

excerpt.text:
Divide array in half
Recursively sort both sides
Merge the two sorted sides

topics.pitfall: Merging is linear, not constant time. Include the work done outside recursive calls.

topics.title: Heapsort
topics.summary: Build a max-heap, then place its maximum at the end of the remaining heap repeatedly.
points: The array has two regions: an active max-heap prefix and a sorted suffix.
Build-Max-Heap costs Θ(n); n−1 removals and repairs cost O(n log n). Worst-case total Θ(n log n); in-place, generally unstable.
topics.formula: Θ(n) + O(n log n) = O(n log n); worst case Θ(n log n)

excerpt.text: Uses Build-Heap instead of inserting elements into heap one by one

topics.pitfall: Decrease heap size before heapifying; otherwise the sorted suffix can be pulled back into the heap.
topics.pseudocode:
Build-Max-Heap(A,n)
for j = n downto 2:
  swap(A[1],A[j])
  A.heapsize = A.heapsize − 1
  Max-Heapify(A,1)

topics.title: Generic Priority Queue sort
topics.summary: Insert all input elements into a separate max-priority queue, then extract maxima into the array from right to left.
points: This is an algorithm template: its runtime depends on the priority queue implementation.
Unsorted linked-list PQ: Θ(n²) total. Binary-heap PQ: Θ(n log n) worst-case total.
topics.formula: Total = n insertions + n Extract-Max operations
topics.example: Input [2,9,4]: extract 9 into A[3], 4 into A[2], 2 into A[1], obtaining [2,4,9].

excerpt.text: Insert elements of A into a PQ // Don’t change array A

topics.pitfall: Writing extracted maxima left to right produces descending order, not ascending order.

topics.title: Quicksort
topics.summary: Partition around a pivot, then recursively sort the elements on its two sides.
points: Partition runs in Θ(n) and puts the pivot in its final sorted position. The two sides need not themselves be sorted yet.
Balanced splits give Θ(n log n). Choosing the last element on sorted distinct input gives Θ(n²). Standard in-place partitioning is not stable.
topics.example: [4,2,8,3,9,1,7,5], pivot 5: the low side contains {1,2,3,4}, then 5, then {7,8,9}. Recurse on the two sides.

excerpt.text: Pick an element x of the array. Call it the “pivot”

topics.pitfall: Exclude the pivot from both recursive calls. Partitioning alone does not sort either side.

topics.title: Randomized-Quicksort
topics.summary: Choose the pivot uniformly at random in every recursive subarray.
points: For distinct sorted ranks z₁<…<zₙ, zᵢ and zⱼ are compared iff the first pivot from ranks i through j is one of the endpoints.
Expected Θ(n log n) time for every fixed distinct-key input. An unlucky execution can still take Θ(n²).
topics.formula: P(zᵢ compared with zⱼ) = 2/(j−i+1); E[C] = Σᵢ<ⱼ 2/(j−i+1)
topics.example: Ranks 2 and 5 are compared with probability 2/4 = 1/2: whichever of ranks 2,3,4,5 becomes a pivot first decides.

excerpt.text: We will prove that expected runtime of Randomized Quicksort is θ(n log n)

topics.pitfall: The expectation is over pivot choices, not a random input distribution. Naive two-way partitioning needs care with many equal keys.

title: Decision tree lower bounds
description: Why every comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.

topics.title: The Ω(n log n) sorting lower bound
topics.summary: A comparison sorting algorithm must distinguish all n! possible orders of distinct keys.
points: Each internal decision-tree node is a comparison; its two branches are possible outcomes for distinct keys. Each leaf fixes an output ordering.
At least n! leaves are necessary. A binary tree of height h has at most 2ʰ leaves, hence h≥log₂(n!).
Because log₂(n!)=Θ(n log n), some input needs Ω(n log n) comparisons. Mergesort and heapsort match this asymptotically.
topics.example: For n=4, there are 24 orders. Height 4 permits only 16 leaves, so at least one input requires ≥5 comparisons.

excerpt.text: There must be one leaf for every possible permutation of elements of A

topics.pitfall: This is a worst-case lower bound in the comparison model. It does not rule out counting sort using key values directly.

title: Mathematical toolkit
description: Growth rates, logarithmic depth, and the sums behind algorithm analysis.

topics.title: Asymptotic notation
topics.summary: Compare growth rates while ignoring fixed multiplicative constants and a finite initial range.
points: O is an eventual upper bound; Ω is an eventual lower bound; Θ means both.
For eventually positive functions: f=o(g) if f/g→0, and f=ω(g) if f/g→∞.
An O bound need not be tight. Θ is the appropriate notation when both bounds have been proved.
topics.example: 3n²+7n+4 is Θ(n²), O(n³), and o(n³). It is not Θ(n³).

excerpt.text: Remove lower order terms and multiplicative constants

topics.pitfall: O is not synonymous with worst case: you can express best-, average-, or worst-case functions using O.

topics.title: Logarithms
topics.summary: A logarithm answers how many times a base must multiply itself to reach a value.
points: For fixed bases greater than 1, changing the base changes only a constant factor.
A logarithm turns products into sums and powers into multipliers. It does not turn sums into sums of logs.
topics.formula: log_b x = ln x / ln b; log_b(xy)=log_b x+log_b y; log_b(xᵏ)=k log_b x
topics.example: log₂ 32=5; log₂(n²)=2 log₂ n; log₂ n and log₁₀ n are Θ of one another.

excerpt.text: change of base formula

topics.pitfall: log(a+b) is generally not log a + log b. Also, (log n)² and log(n²) grow differently.

topics.title: Repeated halving and doubling
topics.summary: Multiplicative changes lead to a logarithmic number of steps.
points: After k halvings, size is n/2ᵏ. Set this equal to 1 to find the depth.
After k doublings from 1, size is 2ᵏ. Reaching at least n requires ⌈log₂ n⌉ doublings.
topics.example: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 takes 6 halvings. A recursion tree has 7 levels if the root is level 0.

excerpt.text: How many days until you are down to only $1?

topics.pitfall: Distinguish the number of edges/halvings from the number of levels, which includes the starting level.

topics.title: Geometric series
topics.summary: When each term is a fixed multiple of the previous one, the ratio tells you which levels dominate.
points: For fixed r>1, a finite positive sum is Θ of its last term. For fixed 0≤r<1, it is Θ of its first term.
When r=1, multiply the common term by the number of terms. An infinite geometric series converges only when |r|<1.
topics.formula: Σᵢ₌₀ᵏ arⁱ = a(rᵏ⁺¹−1)/(r−1), r≠1; Σᵢ₌₀∞ arⁱ = a/(1−r), |r|<1

excerpt.text: finite geometric series

topics.pitfall: A finite geometric sum and an infinite one have different formulas. Include the i=0 term and count k+1 terms.

topics.title: Harmonic series
topics.summary: The first n reciprocals grow logarithmically even though each new term becomes smaller.
points: The infinite harmonic series diverges. Its finite partial sum Hₙ is Θ(log n).
Grouping terms into blocks [2ᵏ,2ᵏ⁺¹−1] gives Θ(1) per block and Θ(log n) blocks.
topics.example: H₄=1+1/2+1/3+1/4=25/12. In randomized quicksort, sums of reciprocal rank distances produce log n.

excerpt.text: Does this series converge? No.

topics.pitfall: Terms approaching zero do not imply the infinite series converges.

topics.title: Sum of numbers from 1 to n
topics.summary: Pair the first and last terms to turn a growing sum into a closed formula.
points: Each pair from opposite ends sums to n+1. There are n/2 pairs, allowing the middle term when n is odd.
Triangular loops often perform this many iterations.
topics.example: 1+2+3+4+5 = 5·6/2 = 15. Bubblesort comparisons stop at n−1, giving n(n−1)/2.

excerpt.text: Never forget, the sum of the numbers from 1 to n is

topics.pitfall: Check the endpoint: summing to n−1 changes the exact answer even though the Θ bound stays quadratic.

topics.title: The sum of i/2ⁱ
topics.summary: Exponential decay dominates the linear numerator, so the infinite sum is a constant.
points: Differentiate Σxⁱ=1/(1−x) and multiply by x to obtain Σixⁱ=x/(1−x)².
Substitute x=1/2. This sum also bounds the aggregate cost of Build-Max-Heap.

excerpt.text: Differentiate both sides wrt x, get

topics.pitfall: The finite sum is less than 2, not exactly 2. The equality to 2 applies to the infinite sum.

title: Probability
description: Turn repeated trials and event counts into expectations.

topics.title: Expected flips until heads
topics.summary: For independent trials with success probability p, the expected waiting time for the first success is 1/p.
points: For a fair coin, P(X=k)=(1/2)ᵏ: k−1 tails followed by one head. Therefore E[X]=Σk/2ᵏ=2.
A first-step equation gives E[X]=1+(1−p)E[X], so E[X]=1/p.
If flips are capped at m, use Σᵢ₌₁ᵐ (1−p)ⁱ⁻¹ instead.
topics.example: Stop on heads or after 4 flips: expected flips = 1+1/2+1/4+1/8 = 15/8.

excerpt.text: Expected number of trials to get first success is 1/p

topics.pitfall: Include the successful flip. For a cap of 4, P(X=4)=1/8 because both TTTH and TTTT stop after 4 flips.

topics.title: Indicator random variables
topics.summary: Represent an event by 1 when it occurs and 0 otherwise, then sum indicators to count events.
points: If I is an indicator for event E, E[I]=P(E).
Linearity says E[ΣIᵢ]=ΣE[Iᵢ], even when the indicators are dependent.
Pick the event carefully: the indicator that flip i occurs is different from the indicator that flip i is heads.
topics.example: With at most 4 flips until heads, I₃=1 exactly when the first two flips are tails, so E[I₃]=1/4.

excerpt.text:
Y = 1 if event occurs
Y = 0 if event does not occur

topics.pitfall: Independence is not required for linearity of expectation. It is required for certain product probability calculations.

title: Recurrence relations
description: Translate recursive work into a bound, then justify the bound.

topics.title: Master Theorem — the course version
topics.summary: The lecture theorem applies to equal-size subproblems and a polynomial nonrecursive term.
points: Assume T(n)=aT(n/b)+Θ(nᵈ), constant-size base cost Θ(1), and constants a>0, b>1, d≥0.
Compare d with log_b a. Smaller d means leaves dominate; equality means every level contributes equally; larger d means root work dominates.
This version does not directly cover a toll n log n or unequal splits T(n/3)+T(2n/3). Use another method.
topics.formula:
d<log_b a: Θ(n^(log_b a))
d=log_b a: Θ(nᵈ log n)
d>log_b a: Θ(nᵈ)
topics.example: 3T(n/2)+n: d=1<log₂3 → Θ(n^(log₂3)). 2T(n/2)+n → Θ(n log n). 2T(n/2)+n² → Θ(n²).

excerpt.text: a, b, d, n0 are constants

topics.pitfall: Do not use a more general textbook case to claim this course theorem directly handles n log n tolls. Floors/ceilings are accommodated as explained on lecture page 29.

topics.title: Recursion tree analysis
topics.summary: Draw the recursive calls, label only the local work at each node, and sum across all levels.
points: At depth i for aT(n/b)+cnᵈ, there are aⁱ nodes of size n/bⁱ. Local work for the whole level is cnᵈ(a/bᵈ)ⁱ.
Depth is log_b n for powers of b; there are a^(log_b n)=n^(log_b a) leaves. Include their base costs.
topics.formula: Level i work = cnᵈ(a/bᵈ)ⁱ; total = internal-level sum + leaf costs
topics.example: T(n)=2T(n/2)+n, T(1)=1: log₂ n internal levels each cost n, and n leaves cost n; T(n)=n log₂ n+n.

excerpt.text: Method 1: Using Recursion Tree to Solve Recurrence

topics.pitfall: Do not label a node with both T(size) and its local cost when summing; that counts recursive work twice.

topics.title: Solving recurrences by induction
topics.summary: Guess a concrete inequality, prove enough base cases, and substitute the inductive hypothesis.
points: Use an explicit constant in the hypothesis, such as T(k)≤ck log₂k. Big-O notation hides the constant you need to preserve.
Check every recursive argument is covered by the hypothesis. Floors may require more than one base case.
For an exact solution on powers of 2, prove T(n)=n log₂n+n by substituting the half-size formula.
topics.example: Base n=1: 1=1·0+1. For n>1, the displayed substitution establishes the formula for 2T(n/2)+n.

excerpt.text: Important not to use asymptotic notation in the inductive hypothesis!

topics.pitfall: Proving 2·O(n/2)+O(n)=O(n) does not prove T(n)=O(n): the implicit constant can increase at every recursion level.

title: Other algorithms
description: Two divide-and-conquer examples with very different recurrences.

topics.title: Maximum-sum subarray
topics.summary: Find the largest sum of a contiguous segment. In this course, the empty subarray is allowed and has sum 0.
points: An optimum lies wholly left, wholly right, or crosses the midpoint.
A crossing segment combines the maximum-sum suffix of the left half and maximum-sum prefix of the right half. Each can be scanned in linear time.
Brute-force recomputation takes Θ(n³); reusing running sums gives Θ(n²); the lecture divide-and-conquer algorithm gives Θ(n log n).
topics.example: [3,−6,2,3,−5,1,3,−7] has maximum sum 5, achieved by [2,3]. For [−4,−2], the course answer is 0 (empty subarray).

excerpt.text: The empty subarray is also considered to be a subarray. Sum of its elements is 0.

topics.pitfall: A subarray must be contiguous. Ignoring crossing subarrays makes the divide-and-conquer algorithm incorrect.

topics.title: Karatsuba’s algorithm
topics.summary: Multiply two long integers using three recursive products instead of four.
points: Write x=x_L·B+x_R and y=y_L·B+y_R, where B=2^(n/2).
Compute p=x_Ly_L, q=x_Ry_R, r=(x_L+x_R)(y_L+y_R). The cross term is r−p−q.
Additions, subtractions and shifts take Θ(n) bit operations; the lecture recurrence suppresses small carry/rounding details.

excerpt.text: Recursively compute 3 products instead of 4

topics.pitfall: The speedup is in bit-operation complexity for long integers. Treating arbitrary-length multiplication as O(1) would erase the problem.

title: Heaps
description: The array representation and the repair operations behind heapsort and priority queues.

topics.title: Max-Heapify
topics.summary: Repair a possible violation at one node when both child subtrees are already max-heaps.
points: A max-heap is a complete binary tree with each parent key at least each child key. In a 1-indexed array, parent(i)=⌊i/2⌋ and children are 2i and 2i+1.
Compare the node with its valid children, swap with the largest if needed, then continue down that child.
Worst-case time is O(h) for subtree height h, and O(log n) for the full heap.

excerpt.text: Assumes that the left and right subtrees of node i are max-heaps

topics.pitfall: Swapping with the smaller child can leave the parent smaller than its other child. Check bounds against heap size, not array length.

topics.title: Build-Max-Heap
topics.summary: Turn an arbitrary array into a max-heap by heapifying internal nodes from bottom to top.
points: Indices ⌊n/2⌋+1 through n are leaves and already satisfy the heap property.
Process i=⌊n/2⌋ down to 1, so both child subtrees are heaps before calling Max-Heapify.
Most nodes are near the leaves and cheap to repair: summing costs by height gives Θ(n).
topics.example: [1,2,3,4]: heapify index 2 → [1,4,3,2]; heapify index 1 → [4,2,3,1].

excerpt.text: for i = ⌊n/2⌋ downto 1

topics.pitfall: Multiplying n calls by O(log n) gives a valid loose upper bound, but misses the tight Θ(n) analysis.

topics.title: Extract-Max
topics.summary: Remove the root and restore the heap by moving the last active element to the root and bubbling down.
points: Save the root, move the last heap element to position 1, decrease heap size, and call Max-Heapify at 1.
Worst-case Θ(log n), with heap underflow on an empty heap. Handles must be updated if the heap stores objects.
topics.example: [9,7,8,1,3] returns 9. Move 3 to root → [3,7,8,1]; heapify → [8,7,3,1].

excerpt.text: max = Max-Heap-Maximum(A)

topics.pitfall: Return the saved original maximum, not the new root after repair.

topics.title: Maximum
topics.summary: Read the largest key at the root without removing it.
points: The heap property implies every descendant has key at most the root key.
For a nonempty 1-indexed max-heap, simply return A[1]. Time Θ(1).
topics.example: In heap [20,12,18,3,7], Maximum returns 20 and leaves all five entries in place.

excerpt.text: return max element, don’t delete

topics.pitfall: Maximum and Extract-Max have different effects and different runtimes. Neither implies the heap array is fully sorted.

title: Priority queues
description: An abstract interface, two implementations, and the bookkeeping needed to find an object.

topics.title: Priority queue operations
topics.summary: Maintain elements with priority keys and retrieve the element with greatest priority.
points: Insert(S,x,k) adds x with key k. Maximum(S) returns the highest-priority element without deletion.
Extract-Max removes and returns that element. Increase-Key raises an existing element’s key and restores the data structure.
The abstract data type specifies behavior; its implementation determines cost.
topics.example: Insert (job A,2), (job B,7). Maximum returns B. Increase A to 9, then Extract-Max removes A.

excerpt.text: Each element has a number, called a key, indicating its priority

topics.pitfall: An element’s identity and its key are different. Two distinct jobs can have the same priority.

topics.title: Doubly-linked list implementation
topics.summary: An unordered doubly-linked list makes insertion and known-element updates cheap, but maximum queries expensive.
points: Insert at the front in Θ(1). Maximum scans all n keys in Θ(n).
Extract-Max scans in Θ(n), then unlinks the chosen node in Θ(1).
Increase-Key is Θ(1) when given the node or when mapping cost is excluded; finding an element by a linear scan would add Θ(n).
topics.formula: Unordered DLL: Insert Θ(1), Max Θ(n), Extract-Max Θ(n), Increase-Key Θ(1) excluding lookup
topics.example: For priorities [2,9,4], finding 9 scans the list. Once its node is known, prev/next links remove it in constant time.

excerpt.text: Example: Implementation of PQ using unsorted doubly-linked list

topics.pitfall: Do not confuse the unordered list here with a sorted list; ordering the list changes which operations are cheap.

topics.title: Heap implementation
topics.summary: A binary max-heap balances efficient insertion, extraction, and priority increases.
points: Maximum is Θ(1). Extract-Max, Insert, and Increase-Key have O(log n) worst-case costs, excluding mapping.
Increase-Key locates x, changes its key, then bubbles up while the parent is smaller.
Insert appends a new leaf (conceptually with key −∞), then increases it to its intended key.
topics.formula: Heap: Insert O(log n), Max Θ(1), Extract-Max O(log n), Increase-Key O(log n)

excerpt.text:
Locate x in heap (using mapping operation)
Increase key of x to k
Need to repair heap!

topics.pitfall: An increase bubbles upward; replacing the root after extraction bubbles downward. Using the wrong direction does not repair the heap.

topics.title: Handles and mapping operations
topics.summary: Keep a way to locate an object after heap swaps move it to a different array index.
points: A handle may carry an index, or a separate dictionary may map object identity to its current index.
Every swap must update the positions of both affected objects; deletion must invalidate or remove the deleted object’s entry.
The lecture excludes mapping-operation costs from quoted PQ runtimes. State that assumption when comparing implementations.
topics.formula: Invariant: position[A[i].id] = i for every active heap index i
topics.example: Swap A[2]=job X and A[5]=job Y: update position[X]=5 and position[Y]=2 before the next Increase-Key lookup.

excerpt.text: Handle must be updated when elements move during operations on the heap

topics.pitfall: A stale index can update the wrong job even if the heap still satisfies the heap property.
